pages.title: Usage
pages.description: Installation, first copy, and command reference.
pages.body:
`waft` copies selected Git-ignored files from the main worktree to a linked
worktree in the same repository. By default, it leaves existing destination
files alone.

## Installation

`waft` is not published to crates.io. Install a reviewed commit from Git:

```sh
cargo install --git https://github.com/plx/waft \
  --rev REVIEWED_COMMIT_SHA --locked waft
```

Replace `REVIEWED_COMMIT_SHA` with the full SHA of the commit you reviewed.

## Quick start

1. Add `.worktreeinclude` at the root of the main worktree. For example, to
   copy local environment files:

   ```text
   .env
   *.env.local
   ```

   These files must already exist and be ignored by Git. Listing a tracked
   file here does not make it eligible.

2. From a linked worktree, preview the copy:

   ```sh
   waft copy --dry-run
   ```

3. Review the plan, then copy:

   ```sh
   waft copy
   ```

From a linked worktree, the source and destination are automatic. To name
them explicitly:

```sh
waft copy --source /path/to/main --dest /path/to/linked
```

The source must be the main worktree. From there, pass `--dest` to choose a
linked worktree. `waft` does not create worktrees or copy between repositories.

With the default profile, a missing `.worktreeinclude` selects nothing. Use
`waft info .env` to check why a file is selected or skipped. See
[file selection](../worktreeinclude/) for matching rules.

## Commands

| Command               | Description                                       |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `waft` / `waft copy`  | Copy eligible files. This is the default command. |
| `waft list`           | List eligible files without copying.              |
| `waft info <PATH>...` | Show detailed status for specific files.          |
| `waft validate`       | Check `.worktreeinclude` and Git ignore syntax.   |

## Global options

| Option                                          | Description                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--source <PATH>`                               | Source, usually the main worktree path.                     |
| `--dest <PATH>`                                 | Destination, usually the linked worktree path.              |
| `-C <PATH>`                                     | Operate as if started in `PATH`.                            |
| `-q, --quiet`                                   | Suppress non-error output.                                  |
| `-v, --verbose`                                 | Increase output verbosity.                                  |
| `--copy-strategy <auto\|simple-copy\|cow-copy>` | Select plain-copy or copy-on-write behavior.                |
| `--isolated`                                    | Omit user config and `WAFT_*` policy environment variables. |

## Copy options

| Option          | Description                                                                                                                       |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-n, --dry-run` | Show what would be done without copying.                                                                                          |
| `--overwrite`   | Replace untracked destinations that differ, and repair untracked destinations whose content matches but whose permissions do not. |

## Copy output

A copy run reports each published file (`copied:`, `replaced:`,
`repaired permissions:`) and each file it left alone, with the reason:

```text
skip: .env (untracked conflict; --overwrite replaces the destination)
```

Skips are not failures; the run still exits 0. `--quiet` suppresses all of it
except per-file failures.

If the active configuration selects nothing and no `.worktreeinclude` was
consulted, `copy`, `list`, and `info` say so once on standard error:

```text
note: no .worktreeinclude found; the claude profile selects nothing without one (see waft validate)
```

The note names whatever is responsible, so it also covers a rule file that
exists but is never read — one outside the repository root under root-only
`claude-2026-04` semantics, or a symlinked one under
`--worktreeinclude-symlink-policy ignore`. A consulted rule file that
legitimately matches nothing is not flagged. Standard output stays
machine-readable, and `--quiet` suppresses the note. Symlink hints ask you to
inspect targets and validate with the intended settings. They do not promise
that changing policy will validate or select files.

See [Configuration](../configuration/) for profile, exclusion, and config-file
options, and [Safety](../safety/) for conflict handling.

## Optional post-checkout hook

Install the repository's post-checkout hook from a reviewed source checkout:

```sh
just install-hooks
```

The installer builds `waft`, copies the binary and hook into the repository's
common Git directory, and configures an absolute `core.hooksPath`. The hook
uses the pinned binary with `--isolated`; source-project configuration still
applies. The installer refuses symlinked prior hooks and worktree-specific
hook overrides.

Reinstall the hook after upgrading `waft`. Remove it and restore the previous
hook configuration with:

```sh
just uninstall-hooks
```

Do not point `core.hooksPath` at the tracked `hooks/` directory. A checked-out
branch can replace that directory before Git runs the hook.

pages.title: .worktreeinclude
pages.description: Which files to copy and how patterns match.
pages.body:
Put `.worktreeinclude` at the root of the main worktree to select ignored
files for copying. The default `claude` profile uses `.gitignore`-style
patterns:

```text
# Local environment files
.env
*.env.local

# Except test environments
!test.env.local
```

This file selects files; it does not make Git ignore them. In this example,
`.env` and matching local environment files must already be ignored and untracked.

## Eligibility

A file is eligible for copying only when all of these are true:

1. It exists in the source worktree.
2. It is a regular file, not a symlink, directory, or special file.
3. It is selected by the active compatibility profile.
4. Git confirms it is ignored and untracked.
5. It is not removed by a built-in or configured exclusion.

## Profile-dependent matching

The default `claude` profile reads only the repository root
`.worktreeinclude`. The `git` profile composes nested `.worktreeinclude` files
like nested `.gitignore` files. The `wt` profile starts with every ignored,
untracked file and applies worktrunk-compatible exclusions.

Without a root `.worktreeinclude`, the default profile selects nothing.
See [Profiles](../profiles/) for the differences and how to choose one.

## Validation

Run `waft validate` to check rule-file syntax or `waft info .env` to see why a
particular file is selected or skipped.

pages.title: Safety
pages.description: Existing files, symlinks, and concurrent changes.
pages.body:
`waft` copies missing files and preserves existing destinations by default.
Preview the copy with:

```sh
waft copy --dry-run
```

The preview reports files to copy, skip, or leave as up-to-date. With
`--overwrite`, it also reports replacements and permission repairs. It writes
nothing. A later `waft copy` builds a new plan from the current state.

## Existing files

**Tracked files are never overwritten.** Without `--overwrite`, matching files
are reported as up-to-date and conflicts are skipped. Skips are not failures;
the run names each skipped file and its reason, and still exits 0:

```text
skip: .env (untracked conflict; --overwrite replaces the destination)
```

On Unix, `--overwrite` acts on untracked destinations in two cases:

- **Untracked conflict:** content differs. The replacement is prepared in a
  temporary file, then published as `replaced:`.
- **Content equal, permissions differ:** the mode is repaired on the verified
  file descriptor without rewriting content, reported as `repaired permissions:`.

```sh
waft copy --overwrite
```

Both actions check the destination against the identity, length, content
fingerprint, and mode observed while planning. A detected change is a per-file
failure; the rest of the run continues. Windows has no supported overwrite
or permission-repair path.

## Before each write

- Destination tracked status is checked during planning and again under Git's
  index lock before the file is put in place.
- Source symlinks are not copied. On Unix, source and destination paths are
  opened relative to worktree directory handles with `O_NOFOLLOW`.
- File contents are synced to a temporary file before publication. Parent
  directories are synced on Unix. Missing destinations use no-clobber publication.
- Replacements use atomic exchange where supported. The checked
  displacement/no-clobber fallback can leave a temporary gap at the destination
  and named recovery files.

**The whole copy is not a transaction.** If one file fails, files already
copied remain in the destination. Recovery restores a displaced file or
preserves it at a named recovery path when restoring would clobber a later
writer. Cleanup failures name surviving recovery paths.

## Concurrent changes

Normal Git writers honor the index lock and cannot change tracked status
between the final check and the write. Direct index edits that ignore Git's
lock protocol are outside this guarantee.

On Unix, directory handles prevent symlink or name swaps from redirecting a
write. Another process can still move an already-open destination directory
after the final check. Avoid moving destination directories during a copy.

`waft` reacquires the index lock for each published file and reuses a cached
tracked-path snapshot while the index fingerprint stays unchanged. A changed
index triggers a reload. Keep automatic manifests narrow and benchmark your
own workload.

Unix signal cleanup attempts to remove owned index locks on `SIGINT` and
`SIGTERM`, but staging files can survive termination. Crashes and `SIGKILL`
can leave stale locks as well. Inspect recovery files and establish that no
Git writer is active before removing a stale lock.

## Automatic copies

The optional [post-checkout hook](../usage/#optional-post-checkout-hook) uses a
pinned binary with `--isolated`. User config and `WAFT_*` policy variables do
not affect it; source-project configuration still does.

Install the hook from a reviewed revision. Do not set `core.hooksPath` to a
directory inside a checked-out worktree: branches can replace tracked hook
content before Git invokes it.

## Local credentials

Copying an environment file or credential creates another copy readable by
anything with access to the destination. Select only the files that worktree
needs.

pages.title: Profiles
pages.description: The differences between claude, git, and wt.
pages.body:
Profiles control how `.worktreeinclude` is interpreted. The default is `claude`. Use `git` for nested rule files or `wt` for the Worktrunk behavior described below. ```sh waft copy --compat-profile git --dry-run ``` Each profile sets four options together:
Profile Missing .worktreeinclude Matcher semantics Symlinked rule files Tool-state excludes
claude nothing selected claude-2026-04 follow none
git nothing selected git ignore none
wt every git-ignored untracked file selected wt-0.39 follow tooling-v1
## `claude` `claude` is the default. It reads only the repository root `.worktreeinclude` and matches the observed Claude Code behavior identified by `claude-2026-04`. ## `git` `git` applies per-directory exclude semantics. Patterns are relative to the directory containing the rule file, and deeper rule files override shallower ones. ## `wt` `wt` matches the observed Worktrunk behavior identified by `wt-0.39`. It starts with every ignored, untracked file, even without `.worktreeinclude`, and removes paths matched by literal-name negations. Positive patterns and glob negations are ignored. The `tooling-v1` exclusion set also removes tool state such as `.claude/` and `.conductor/`. These are versioned compatibility behaviors, not a promise to match future Claude Code or Worktrunk releases. [Configuration](../configuration/) lists the individual overrides.

pages.title: Configuration
pages.description: Config files, environment variables, and CLI overrides.
pages.body:
Put project settings in `.waft.toml` in the main worktree. For example, to
use nested include rules and exclude backup files:

```toml
version = 1

[compat]
profile = "git"

[exclude]
extra = ["*.bak"]
```

## Precedence

`waft` applies configuration in the following order. Later values
override earlier ones, except for extra exclusions, which append.

1. Built-in defaults.
2. User config: `~/.config/waft/config.toml`.
3. Project configs: each `.waft.toml` in the resolved source worktree, from
   its repo root down to the invocation directory's equivalent source path.
4. Environment variables using the `WAFT_*` prefix.
5. CLI flags.

`exclude.extra` arrays append across layers. Set
`exclude.replace_extra = true` or pass `--replace-extra-excludes` to discard
values from earlier layers.

Project configs must be regular files. Symlinked configs cause an error, and
discovery stops at nested repositories and registered submodules.

Selecting a profile resets its four settings at that layer. Explicit settings
in the same or a later layer can override it.

`--isolated` omits user configuration, `WAFT_CONFIG_PATH`, and `WAFT_*` policy
environment variables. Built-in defaults, source-project configuration, CLI
overrides, and Git backend selection still apply.
It conflicts with `--config`.

## CLI overrides

| Option                                                       | Description                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--compat-profile <claude\|git\|wt>`                         | Apply a compatibility profile.                            |
| `--when-missing-worktreeinclude <blank\|all-ignored>`        | Set behavior when no `.worktreeinclude` exists.           |
| `--worktreeinclude-semantics <claude-2026-04\|git\|wt-0.39>` | Select the matcher.                                       |
| `--worktreeinclude-symlink-policy <follow\|ignore\|error>`   | Set handling for symlinked rule files.                    |
| `--builtin-exclude-set <none\|tooling-v1>`                   | Select a built-in exclusion set.                          |
| `--extra-exclude <GLOB>`                                     | Add an exclusion. Repeat the option to add more than one. |
| `--replace-extra-excludes`                                   | Discard exclusions inherited from earlier layers.         |
| `--copy-strategy <auto\|simple-copy\|cow-copy>`              | Select plain-copy or copy-on-write behavior.              |
| `--config <PATH>`                                            | Replace user-config discovery with the specified file.    |
| `--isolated`                                                 | Omit user config and policy environment variables.        |

pages.title: Architecture
pages.description: How the code selects and copies files.
pages.body:
`waft` uses Git to check file status, `.worktreeinclude` to select files, and a
copy plan to separate those reads from writes.

## Git backends

The `GitBackend` trait supplies final ignored and tracked status. `waft` does
not infer either status from `.gitignore` parsing alone.

- `GitGix` is the default in-process backend built on the `gix` crate.
- `GitCli` runs Git commands. Select it with `WAFT_GIT_BACKEND=cli`.

## File matching

`worktreeinclude_engine` applies `.worktreeinclude` rules independently of the
Git backend. It provides three matchers:

- `claude-2026-04`, the default root-rule-file behavior.
- `git`, Git-style per-directory exclude semantics.
- `wt-0.39`, worktrunk-compatible subtractive behavior.

## Command pipeline

The pipeline is read-only through copy planning.

1. Parse CLI arguments.
2. Resolve source and destination worktree context.
3. Resolve layered policy against that source worktree.
4. Validate ignore files.
5. Select candidate files.
6. Apply policy filters.
7. Confirm ignored status through Git.
8. Build a copy plan.
9. For `copy` without `--dry-run`, verify planned state and publish each file.
   An existing pathname is replaced only under `--overwrite`, only when it is
   untracked, and only after it still matches the state recorded while
   planning.

`validate` stops after rule parsing. `list` and `info` stop after
classification. `copy --dry-run` stops after planning.

The planner and executor live in `src/planner.rs` and `src/executor.rs`.
See [Safety](../safety/) for the checks made before each write.
